newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy faces hard budget sell after Chirac comments.
newsitem.headline: Italy faces hard budget sell after Chirac comments.

text.p: Italy's anger at French suggestions that it may trip up in a race to join a single European currency stems from fears that a tough budget unveiled last week could now be impossible to sell to a sceptical public.
French President Jacques Chirac caused a storm on Tuesday when he said Italy might not be among the first countries to join a single European currency.
He quickly retracted his comments, made just two days before a Franco-Italian summit, saying he hoped Italy would be in the first wave after all but analysts said the damage was already done.

Chirac's remarks were acutely embarrassing for Prime Minister Romano Prodi who last week unveiled a tough 1997 budget with the promise it would win Italy a place in an advance party of nations joining European economic and monetary union in 1999.

"The government's bluff has been called almost immediately," said Giovanna Mossetti, an economist at Milan brokerage Caboto. "It looks like they made a huge mistake by selling something to the public they did not already have."

The Chirac incident brought more discomfort to an Italian government already shaken after the Financial Times of London quoted Spanish premier Jose Maria Aznar as saying Prodi tried to enlist his support in a bid to wring milder terms for EMU membership.
This prompted the Italian premier to issue a firm denial and to hold a telephone conversation with Aznar to make amends.

Prodi unveiled an unusually stringent budget last week, including a 13 trillion lire ($8.55 billion) once-off "Euro tax", in a dramatic policy turnaround after earlier resisting calls for punitive tax measures.

The budget aims to lop 62.5 trillion lire off Italy's public sector deficit and put it on track to meet one of the key qualifying criteria for EMU -- a deficit to gross domestic product (GDP) ratio of three percent by the end of 1997.

The package of measures won high praise from financial markets, which soared on the news, but drew criticism from economists who say the fiscal screws are being tightened too hard while generous welfare state provisions are left unscathed.

Prodi was galvanised into forging ahead with an uncompromising budget only after he belatedly realised that France and Spain were determined to do all in their power to meet the three percent deficit to GDP target.
"We have to recognise that our governors have acted a bit clumsily," political scientist Gianfranco Pasquino said in an interview with Corriere della Sera.

"The Prodi government started to look for allies prepared to help us to slow down the march towards monetary Europe and only in his recent visit to Spain did the prime minister discover with disappointment these allies are not there," added Pasquino.
Finance Minister Vincenzo Visco raised the temperature on Monday when he said some of Italy's partners did not want the country in EMU although on Tuesday he denied he had spoken of a "plot".

The challenge the government now faces is to steer through parliament one of the most taxing budgets of recent years when even its closest allies are now openly casting doubt on Italy's chances of claiming a berth on the first EMU boat.
"People are going to ask why should we pay all these taxes if we are going to stay out anyway," said an economist with a London-based investment bank, who asked not to be named.
